howard-john-george.name: John George Howard
howard-john-george.title: Architect, Surveyor & Founder of High Park
howard-john-george.bio: Born John Corby in Hertfordshire, England, Howard emigrated to York (Toronto) in 1832 and changed his name soon after. He became the first professional architect in Upper Canada, the city's official surveyor (1843–1855), and a teacher at Upper Canada College. He laid out the Esplanade and subdivided Toronto Island, designed dozens of homes, churches and public buildings, and in 1873 donated the land that became High Park — where he and his wife Jemima are buried near the home he built, Colborne Lodge.
howard-john-george.source: Dictionary of Canadian Biography / Biographical Dictionary of Architects in Canada

stops.name: Colborne Lodge
stops.role: His home, where he died in 1890 — now a museum
stops.address: Colborne Lodge Drive, High Park, Toronto
stops.description: Howard built Colborne Lodge on land he bought in 1836 for a sheep farm. He and his wife Jemima lived here until his death in 1890; both are buried nearby beneath a cairn he designed himself, topped with a fence salvaged from a shipwreck that originally stood around St Paul's Cathedral in London. The house is now a museum displaying Howard's own watercolours and woodcarvings.

stops.name: Provincial Lunatic Asylum
stops.address: Queen St W, opposite Ossington Ave, Toronto
stops.description: Howard's largest commission: an immense building in the white brick he introduced to Toronto building practice, modelled on London's National Gallery. It was the most significant public building of his career, and remained on this site (later expanded as 999 Queen St W) until its demolition in 1976.

stops.role: One of his earliest Toronto commissions — demolished 1946
stops.address: Southeast corner of York & King Streets, Toronto (later site of the Standard Life Centre)
stops.description: Among the first buildings Howard designed after arriving in York in 1832–33, in the wide range of late-Georgian styles typical of his early Toronto practice.

stops.name: Home District Gaol
stops.address: Southeast corner of Front & Berkeley Streets, Toronto
stops.description: As the city's surveyor and a busy public architect, Howard designed several institutional buildings; this jail replaced an earlier 1827 gaol on King Street and stood until 1887.

stops.name: St James' Cemetery
stops.role: Picturesque-style cemetery plan, still in use
stops.address: 635 Parliament Street, north of Wellesley Street East, Toronto
stops.description: Howard surveyed and laid out St James' Cemetery in 1844 — an early Toronto example of the 'picturesque' landscape planning style, in contrast to the gridiron subdivisions he carried out elsewhere in the city.

william-thomas.name: William Thomas
william-thomas.title: Architect, Engineer & Founding President of the Toronto Society of Arts
william-thomas.bio: Born in Suffolk, England, Thomas trained as a carpenter-joiner and builder before becoming an architect, working two decades in Leamington Spa before a building-trade depression sent him to Toronto in 1843. In under two decades he designed and supervised over 100 buildings across Ontario — including some of Toronto's most important 19th-century landmarks — and trained the next generation of architects, including William George Storm. He was a founding president of the Toronto Society of Arts (1847) and, when Howard travelled to England in 1853, served as city engineer in his place, overseeing work on the Esplanade.
william-thomas.source: Dictionary of Canadian Biography / Canadian Encyclopedia

stops.name: Oakham House
stops.role: His own house and office — now part of Toronto Metropolitan University
stops.description: Thomas designed this Gothic Revival house as his own residence and architectural office in 1848, the same year as St Michael's Cathedral. It later housed a working boys' home before being granted to Ryerson (now Toronto Metropolitan University), where it remains the campus's student centre.

stops.name: The Don Jail
stops.role: Toronto's most architecturally ambitious 19th-century jail — now an office building
stops.description: Thomas's design for a new Toronto jail was completed four years after his death in 1860, with William George Storm — his former apprentice and Cumberland's partner — overseeing construction. The building operated as a jail until 1977 and has since been restored as part of the Bridgepoint Health campus.

frederic-cumberland.name: Frederic W. Cumberland
frederic-cumberland.title: Architect, Engineer & Railway Manager
frederic-cumberland.bio: Born in London, England, Cumberland trained as an architect through the British Admiralty's Civil Architects Department before emigrating to Toronto in 1847. In partnership first with Thomas Ridout and then with William George Storm — himself trained under William Thomas — Cumberland designed many of Toronto's most significant Victorian-era buildings. He won the competition for St James' Cathedral in open contest against ten other entrants in 1849, and later balanced his architectural career with work as chief engineer and managing director of the Northern Railway, eventually leaving architecture for railways and politics, serving in both the Ontario legislature and the House of Commons.
frederic-cumberland.source: Dictionary of Canadian Biography / Canadian Encyclopedia

stops.name: Cumberland House ("Pendarves")
stops.role: His home for 21 years — later a vice-regal residence, now U of T's International Student Centre
stops.address: College St & St George St, Toronto
stops.description: Cumberland built this Italianate villa while working on the nearby University College, and lived here for the last third of his life — during which he was elected to the first Ontario legislature (1867) and then to the House of Commons (1871). After 1912 it served as a temporary vice-regal residence; it is now the University of Toronto's International Student Centre.

stops.name: University College
stops.role: His masterwork — the founding college of the University of Toronto
stops.description: Designed with William George Storm in a Norman Romanesque style with irregular massing and skillful stone-carving, University College is considered Cumberland's single best-known and most accomplished work — by one account, his last personal design before turning to railway management.

stops.name: Stewart Observatory
stops.role: Originally the Toronto Magnetic & Meteorological Observatory — one of Canada's first purpose-built scientific observatories
stops.description: Designed by Cumberland & Storm and built on the University of Toronto campus, this small Romanesque observatory housed Toronto's pioneering magnetic and meteorological research. It was later relocated within the campus and renamed for Louis B. Stewart.
